Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India: When Can a Public Authority Be Called “State”?

One of the most important decisions in Indian Administrative Law, R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, transformed the understanding of Article 12 and Article 14 of the Constitution.

The Supreme Court held that the International Airport Authority was an instrumentality and agency of the Central Government and therefore fell within the meaning of “State” under Article 12.

The Court identified several factors relevant to determining whether a body is an instrumentality of the State, including:

• Government financial assistance
• State ownership of share capital
• Degree of governmental control over management and policy
• Monopoly status granted by the State
• Whether the functions are closely related to governmental functions
• Transfer of governmental functions, assets or liabilities

The principles were later developed into the well-known six-factor test in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi.

But the case is equally significant for Article 14 and administrative fairness.

The Airport Authority had prescribed a tender condition requiring bidders to have five years’ registration as a second-class hotelier. Yet, it accepted a tender from a party who did not satisfy that condition.

The Supreme Court emphasized a crucial principle:

A public authority cannot arbitrarily depart from the standards it has itself prescribed.
If an authority announces eligibility conditions and then selectively ignores them, its action may become arbitrary and discriminatory, offending Article 14.

Although the Court found the action arbitrary, it declined to cancel the contract because of the delay in approaching the Court and the substantial investment already made by the successful bidder.

The judgment therefore remains important for two interconnected reasons:
Article 12: It expanded the understanding of State instrumentalities.
Article 14: It reinforced the principle that public authorities must act fairly, consistently and without arbitrariness—even in commercial and contractual matters.

Its influence continues through later decisions such as Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas.

comment: A key practical issue is that Article 14 scrutiny does not disappear in contractual matters. Public bodies gain flexibility, but consistency in applying their own standards remains the real test.
